study.title: Luke 5 - Jesus Authority, Grace to sinners, and the newness of the Kingdom
study.overview: Luke 5 gathers scenes that reveal who Jesus is and how he acts: he teaches with authority, calls unlikely disciples, cleanses a leper, forgives and heals a paralytic, calls Levi, and answers the objections about company and fasting. The chapter not only presents miracles; it shows that the presence of Jesus inaugurates a new reality, in which sin is forgiven, the marginalized are attained and religious structures cannot limit the action of the Kingdom. At the same time, the human response varies between faith, astonishment, murmuring and abandonment of everything to follow him.

outline.title: Wonderful fishing and the call of the first disciples
outline.explanation: Jesus teaches the crowd of Simon's boat, demonstrates authority over creation with abundant fishing and calls Peter and his companions to a new mission: to fish people. Peter's reaction is a consciousness of sin and fear - contrasts with the word of Jesus: "Do not fear."

outline.title: Jesus purifies the leper and withdraws to pray
outline.explanation: A man full of leprosy pleads for the will and power of Jesus, and receives immediate purification when touched. Jesus tells him that healing be witnessed according to the law of Moses, while his fame grows and he departs into desert places to pray.

outline.title: Forgiveness and healing of the paralytic before the religious leaders
outline.explanation: In the midst of the Pharisees and teachers of the law, Jesus sees the faith of men who descend the paralytic from the roof. He first forgives sins, then heals the body, showing that he has the authority to do both; the crowd glorifies God, but the leaders question his speech.

outline.title: Called Levi, table with sinners, fasting and the parable of the new
outline.explanation: Jesus calls Levi, who follows him and offers a banquet with publicans and others. Faced with criticism, Jesus claims that he came to call sinners to repentance and uses images of the bridegroom, the remendo and the wine to explain why his presence and his work do not fit in ancient schemes. The closure shows that whoever is accustomed to the old tends to prefer him.

study.context: The chapter mentions the lake of Genesaré, the life of fishermen, a leper that needed to be isolated according to the guidelines of Moses" law and a publican linked to the collection of taxes. The notes also indicate that the audience includes Pharisees and law instructors from Galilee, Judea, and Jerusalem. The setting shows Jesus acting in both public spaces and homes, in contrast to the expectation of religious leaders.
study.theology: Luke 5 highlights the unique authority of Jesus in four areas: on creation, in ordering fishing; over ritual purity, when touching the leper; upon sins, in declaring forgiveness to the paralytic; and upon the so-called savior, in seeking Levi and sinners. The chapter also teaches that faith is expressed in concrete obedience, as when Peter launches the network for thy word and when the friends of the paralytic persist despite obstacles. The correct answer before Jesus includes humility, reverent fear, repentance, and follow-up. Moreover, the metaphor of new wine shows that the arrival of Jesus is not mere adjustment of old habits, but the introduction of a reality of the Kingdom that requires new wineskins. The last sentence exposes human resistance to God's newness: custom may seem more comfortable than the transforming work of Christ.

scholarViews.insight: Luke records here the first call of disciples in this gospel and highlights the extraordinary authority of Jesus in miraculous fishing and Simon Peter's call.
The leper represents human spiritual impurity; the right attitude is to seek Jesus with humility, recognizing our need for purification.
The final phrase shows that the old is "better" to the taste of those who resist the change; the preference for the old illustrates opposition to the novelty brought by Jesus.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to obey the word of Jesus even when human experience seems to contradict it, as did Peter?
In which areas do you tend to prefer what is known, rather than welcoming the newness of God's action?
How does Jesus" attitude toward leper, paralytic and Levi correct our way of treating people seen as marginal or unworthy?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete area in which you need to rely more on the word of Jesus than in the reading of circumstances itself. It also practice an intentional approach of someone who is usually avoided or labeled, treating this person with dignity, listening and compassion. Finally, examine whether any religious or spiritual routine has only become customary; ask God to renew his heart without losing faithfulness to the gospel.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not accurately detail all historical background, so I avoided stating dates, exact locations or broader reconstructions that are not explicitly supported in them. I also did not extend the sense of technical terms beyond what the notes allow. Luke 5:39's reading as resistance of the religious leaders comes from Tyndale's note; Adam Clarke's emphasizes subjective preference for the old, and both should be read as interpretations, not as an undeniable final definition of the verse.
